import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    confusion_matrix,
    f1_score,
    precision_score,
    recall_score,
)

Get the Vertebral Column Data Set

In [3]:
#initiate the column names at the beginning since they are not available in the raw data
column_names = [
    "pelvic_incidence",
    "pelvic_tilt",
    "lumbar_lordosis_angle",
    "sacral_slope",
    "pelvic_radius",
    "grade_spondylolisthesis",
    "class"
]

data = pd.read_csv(
    "../data/vertebral_column_data/column_2C.dat",
    sep=r"\s+",
    header=None,
    names=column_names
)

data["class"] = data["class"].map({"NO": 0, "AB": 1})

independent_variables = data.columns[:-1].tolist()

(c) Classification¶

i. Euclidean Metric¶

In [7]:
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
    n_neighbors=4,
    metric="euclidean"
)

knn.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred = knn.predict(X_test)

ii. Test Data¶

Test all the data in the test database with k nearest neighbors. Take decisions by majority pollin¶
In [8]:
euclidean_k_values = list(range(208, 0, -3))

euclidean_train_errors = []
euclidean_test_errors = []

for k in euclidean_k_values:
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k,
        metric="euclidean"
    )

    knn.fit(X_train, y_train)

    train_predictions = knn.predict(X_train)
    test_predictions = knn.predict(X_test)

    euclidean_train_errors.append(
        1 - accuracy_score(y_train, train_predictions)
    )

    euclidean_test_errors.append(
        1 - accuracy_score(y_test, test_predictions)
    )

best_euclidean_test_error = min(euclidean_test_errors)
best_euclidean_train_error = min(euclidean_train_errors)

best_euclidean_k = min(
    k for k, error in zip(euclidean_k_values, euclidean_test_errors)
    if error == best_euclidean_test_error
)
Plot train and test errors in terms of k for k ∈ {208,205, . . . ,7,4,1,}(in reverse order)¶

Display Confusion Matrix, true positive rate, true negative rate, precision,and F1-score when k = k∗¶
In [12]:
best_knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
    n_neighbors=k_star_euclidean,
    metric="euclidean"
)

best_knn.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = best_knn.predict(X_test)

cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)

tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()

true_positive_rate = tp / (tp + fn)
true_negative_rate = tn / (tn + fp)
precision = precision_score(y_test, y_pred, pos_label=1)
f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred, pos_label=1)

print(f"True positive rate: {true_positive_rate:.4f}")
print(f"True negative rate: {true_negative_rate:.4f}")

iii. Learning Curve¶

Re-run classifer on subsets of the data of various sizes from 10-210 in increments of 10¶
In [15]:
N_values = list(range(10, 211, 10))

best_test_errors = []
best_k_values = []

training_class_0 = training_set[training_set["class"] == 0]
training_class_1 = training_set[training_set["class"] == 1]

for N in N_values:
    number_class_0 = N // 3
    number_class_1 = N - number_class_0
    
    subset = pd.concat([
        training_class_0.iloc[:number_class_0],
        training_class_1.iloc[:number_class_1]
    ])
    
    X_train_subset = subset[independent_variables]
    y_train_subset = subset["class"]
    
    # For N=200, this produces 1, 6, 11, ..., 196
    candidate_k_values = list(range(1, N, 5))
    
    errors_for_N = []
    
    for k in candidate_k_values:
        knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
            n_neighbors=k,
            metric="euclidean"
        )
        
        knn.fit(X_train_subset, y_train_subset)
        predictions = knn.predict(X_test)
        
        test_error = 1 - accuracy_score(y_test, predictions)
        errors_for_N.append(test_error)
    
    minimum_error = min(errors_for_N)
    
    # Select the smallest k in case of a tie
    optimal_k = min(
        k for k, error in zip(candidate_k_values, errors_for_N)
        if error == minimum_error
    )
    
    best_test_errors.append(minimum_error)
    best_k_values.append(optimal_k)
In [16]:
learning_curve_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "training_size": N_values,
    "optimal_k": best_k_values,
    "best_test_error": best_test_errors
})

In [21]:
log10_p_values = np.arange(0.1, 1.01, 0.1)

minkowski_train_errors = []
minkowski_test_errors = []

for log10_p in log10_p_values:
    p = 10 ** log10_p

    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=best_manhattan_k,
        metric="minkowski",
        p=p
    )

    knn.fit(X_train, y_train)

    train_predictions = knn.predict(X_train)
    test_predictions = knn.predict(X_test)

    minkowski_train_errors.append(
        1 - accuracy_score(y_train, train_predictions)
    )

    minkowski_test_errors.append(
        1 - accuracy_score(y_test, test_predictions)
    )

best_minkowski_test_error = min(minkowski_test_errors)
best_minkowski_train_error = min(minkowski_train_errors)

best_log10_p_minkowski = min(
    log_p
    for log_p, error in zip(log10_p_values, minkowski_test_errors)
    if error == best_minkowski_test_error
)

minkowski_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "log10(p)": np.round(log10_p_values, 1),
    "p": 10 ** log10_p_values,
    "train_error": minkowski_train_errors,
    "test_error": minkowski_test_errors
})

ii. Mahalanobis Distance.¶

In [25]:
X_train_array = X_train.to_numpy(dtype=float)
X_test_array = X_test.to_numpy(dtype=float)

covariance_matrix = np.cov(X_train_array, rowvar=False)
inverse_covariance_matrix = np.linalg.pinv(covariance_matrix)

mahalanobis_train_errors = []
mahalanobis_test_errors = []

for k in k_values:
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k,
        metric="mahalanobis",
        metric_params={"VI": inverse_covariance_matrix},
        algorithm="brute"
    )

    knn.fit(X_train_array, y_train)

    train_predictions = knn.predict(X_train_array)
    test_predictions = knn.predict(X_test_array)

    mahalanobis_train_errors.append(
        1 - accuracy_score(y_train, train_predictions)
    )

    mahalanobis_test_errors.append(
        1 - accuracy_score(y_test, test_predictions)
    )

best_mahalanobis_test_error = min(mahalanobis_test_errors)
best_mahalanobis_train_error = min(mahalanobis_train_errors)

best_mahalanobis_k = min(
    k for k, error in zip(k_values, mahalanobis_test_errors)
    if error == best_mahalanobis_test_error
)

mahalanobis_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "k": k_values,
    "train_error": mahalanobis_train_errors,
    "test_error": mahalanobis_test_errors
})

(e) Weighted Decision¶

Notes: purpose of weighting the distance is to prevent relatively distant neighbors from having the same influence as nearby observations, hence the inverse proportion detail in the instructions.

Weighted Euclidean Distance¶

In [28]:
weighted_euclidean_train_errors = []
weighted_euclidean_test_errors = []

for k in k_values:
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k,
        metric="euclidean",
        weights="distance"
    )

    knn.fit(X_train, y_train)

    train_predictions = knn.predict(X_train)
    test_predictions = knn.predict(X_test)

    weighted_euclidean_train_errors.append(
        1 - accuracy_score(y_train, train_predictions)
    )

    weighted_euclidean_test_errors.append(
        1 - accuracy_score(y_test, test_predictions)
    )

best_weighted_euclidean_test_error = min(weighted_euclidean_test_errors)
best_weighted_euclidean_train_error = min(weighted_euclidean_train_errors)

best_weighted_euclidean_k = min(
    k for k, error in zip(k_values, weighted_euclidean_test_errors)
    if error == best_weighted_euclidean_test_error
)

print("Best weighted Euclidean k:", best_weighted_euclidean_k)
print("Best weighted Euclidean test error:", best_weighted_euclidean_test_error)

The lowest training error achieved in this assignment was 0.00, indicating perfect classification of the training data. This occurred because most methods included (k=1), meaning that each training observation was its own nearest neighbor and was therefore classified correctly. The only method with a nonzero minimum training error was unweighted Minkowski distance. This method used the optimal (k) found for Manhattan distance, which was (k*=6), rather than (k=1). Because each prediction used multiple neighbors, some training error was expected.

Answer

The lowest test error achieved in this assignment was 0.06, with a tie between unweighted Euclidean and unweighted Minkowski distances. When distance-weighted voting was used, the test error increased. This suggests that, for this dataset and train-test split, giving closer neighbors greater voting influence did not improve classification. Uniform voting generalized better because treating all selected neighbors equally produced more accurate test predictions.

In summary, although most methods achieved a training error of 0.00, this did not necessarily make them the best classifiers for unseen data. In fact, unweighted Minkowski KNN had the highest minimum training error but tied for the lowest test error. This demonstrates the important distinction between the two measures: training error reflects how well a model fits the data on which it was trained, whereas test error reflects how well the model generalizes to unseen data.
